content: The relationship between total fat intake and body fatness in children is an important area of study, particularly in the context of preventing childhood overweight and obesity. To better understand this relationship, researchers conducted a systematic review and analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and prospective cohort studies. Below are the findings presented in a detailed, professional manner: 1. Study Design and Scope: The review included RCTs involving children aged 24 months to 18 years, with or without cardiovascular risk factors, who were randomized to either a lower-fat diet (≤30% of total energy intake) or a usual/moderate-fat diet (>30% of total energy intake). These interventions were not aimed at weight loss. Prospective cohort studies were also included if they examined baseline total fat intake and its relationship to weight or body fatness at least 12 months later. Data were collected on weight, body fatness, and blood lipid levels at various time points, ranging from six months to over five years for RCTs, and from baseline to over 10 years for cohort studies. 2. Interventions in RCTs: Three RCTs were included, involving a total of 1,054 children. Two studies recruited children aged 4 to 11 years, while the third included children aged 12 to 13 years. Interventions consisted of dietary counseling and education delivered through individual and group sessions in clinics, schools, and homes. These sessions were conducted by dieticians, nutritionists, behaviorists, or trained teachers. 3. Findings from RCTs: Weight: One study found that dietary counseling to reduce total fat intake may result in little to no difference in weight compared to a usual diet at 12 months (mean difference [MD] -0.50 kg, 95% confidence interval [CI] -1.78 to 0.78; low-quality evidence) and at three years (MD -0.60 kg, 95% CI -2.39 to 1.19; low-quality evidence). Body Mass Index (BMI): Education delivered as a classroom curriculum likely reduced BMI at 17 months (MD -1.5 kg/m², 95% CI -2.45 to -0.55; moderate-quality evidence). However, the effects diminished over time, with no significant difference observed at five years (MD 0 kg/m², 95% CI -0.63 to 0.63; low-quality evidence) or seven years (MD -0.10 kg/m², 95% CI -0.75 to 0.55; low-quality evidence). Cholesterol: Dietary counseling likely resulted in a slight reduction in total cholesterol at 12 months (MD -0.15 mmol/L, 95% CI -0.24 to -0.06; moderate-quality evidence) but had little to no effect over longer periods. LDL cholesterol was also slightly reduced at 12 months (MD -0.12 mmol/L, 95% CI -0.20 to -0.04; moderate-quality evidence) and at five years (MD -0.09 mmol/L, 95% CI -0.17 to -0.01; moderate-quality evidence). However, there was little to no effect on HDL cholesterol or triglycerides at any time point. Height: Lower fat intake may have little to no effect on height at seven years (MD -0.60 cm, 95% CI -2.06 to 0.86; low-quality evidence). 4. Findings from Cohort Studies: A total of 21 prospective cohort studies, involving approximately 25,059 children, were included. Over half of the analyses suggested that higher total fat intake may be associated with increased measures of body fatness. However, the evidence from these studies was highly heterogeneous and of very low quality, making it difficult to draw definitive conclusions. 5. Limitations: The evidence from RCTs was limited by imprecision, poor reporting, and concerns about applicability, particularly due to the inclusion of children with hypercholesterolemia in two trials. The cohort studies were characterized by inconsistent methods and reporting, as well as predominantly very low-quality evidence. Most studies were conducted in high-income countries, limiting the generalizability of findings to lowand middle-income settings. 6. Conclusions: Limited evidence from RCTs suggests that dietary counseling or education to reduce total fat intake (≤30% of total energy) may result in small reductions in BMI, total cholesterol, and LDL cholesterol at certain time points. However, there were no consistent effects on weight, HDL cholesterol, or height. The associations between total fat intake and body fatness in cohort studies were inconsistent and based on very low-quality evidence. High-quality, long-term studies are needed, particularly in lowand middle-income settings, to better understand the potential benefits and harms of reducing total fat intake in children. These findings underscore the need for further research to clarify the role of dietary fat in childhood weight and body fatness, as well as to inform public health strategies aimed at preventing obesity.
